title: Hearsay evidence exceptions - when courts actually admit it
p1:
What if a statement made outside the courtroom can still decide a case?

Most people believe hearsay evidence is always rejected by courts. But that is not the full story.
p2:
Hearsay means a person repeats something they heard from someone else, instead of sharing what they personally witnessed. The concern is that the original speaker cannot be questioned about accuracy.

Yet courts sometimes admit hearsay when circumstances make the statement reliable.
p3:
For example, statements made during an emergency, certain dying declarations, or official records may be accepted because the situation itself provides reasons to trust the information.

The real question is not simply, 'Was this heard from someone else?' Courts ask, 'Is there enough reason to believe this statement is trustworthy?'

A rule designed to prevent unreliable evidence also has carefully created exceptions to ensure genuine facts are not ignored.
conclusion: Did you know courts can admit some hearsay evidence? Which exception do you think makes the most sense?
